issues.body:
`expect(calls).toBe(1)` runs on the next line after `await page.clock.fastForward(5_000)`. `calls` is incremented inside the Node-side route handler; fastForward resolves once the in-page timers have fired, but a retry's fetch still has to cross to the driver before the handler runs. So the exact regression this line exists to catch — endpointRegistryMessage losing `retry: false` for 404/405 and re-arming the 2s chain — can be observed as the pre-retry value and pass.

Secondary, lower confidence: `page.clock.install()` is called in the test body, i.e. after the webPersona auto-fixture has already done `page.goto("/")` (gui/e2e-playwright/support/web-fixtures.ts). Playwright's documented example installs before navigating. On 1.61 install both adds an init script and evaluates into existing frames, so it most likely does take effect here — I could not run the lane to confirm, so I am flagging it as worth pinning rather than asserting it is broken. The polling fix below makes the test correct either way, because it no longer depends on the fake clock being the only thing that can advance the window.

The message-text and muted-class assertions in this test are real; only the "polling stops" half is soft. `expect(listCalls).toBe(0)` in the preceding test is the same class of race, but a far less likely false pass since nothing should be issuing a request at all at that point.
issues.fix_hint: Replace the synchronous read with a window-spanning assertion: `await expect.poll(() => calls, { timeout: 5000 }).toBe(1)`. That is permitted by support/no-timeout-gate.sh (it forbids only waitForTimeout/sleep/setTimeout, not expect.poll) and it removes the dependency on the fake clock being installed early enough — you can then either keep clock.install() or drop it entirely and let the poll span a real 5s window.
issues.title: "polling stops" reads `calls` synchronously after fastForward, so a wrongly re-armed retry can slip past the assertion

issues.body:
`endpointRegistryMessage` is applied only in the poll path; the kill catch falls through to `error.message`, so killError renders the raw QueryRegistryHttpError string.

This is reachable in a normal configuration, and I confirmed the asymmetry on the server: `GET /queries` is READ-gated and `DELETE /queries/{id}` is WRITE-gated (crates/sparq-server/src/http.rs, list_queries_handler / cancel_query_handler), and `auth_gate` leaves reads OPEN when only `--auth-token` is set without `--auth-token-read` — pinned by the `auth_gate_write_only_gates_writes_not_reads` unit test. So an operator on a write-only-gated server can open the monitor with an empty token field, see rows render fine, click Kill, and get "Kill failed (HTTP 401)." with nothing telling them a bearer token is required for the cancel route specifically. Every other gate in this panel is explained; this one is not.
issues.fix_hint: Route the kill catch through the same helper with a kill-specific 401/403 branch, e.g. "Cancel is write-gated — enter the server's bearer token to kill a running query." Keep the existing 404 success-by-race branch ahead of it. A small unit or component case per branch would pin the mapping.
issues.title: A Kill rejected by the WRITE gate surfaces a bare "Kill failed (HTTP 401)." while the equivalent list failure gets an explanatory line

issues.body:
The poll success path calls `setKillError(null)` unconditionally. The poll cadence is 2s and a kill failure does not stop the chain, so the sequence is: Kill fails -> killError renders -> the already-scheduled poll succeeds -> the message is wiped. The operator sees a flash of red under 2s and no lasting explanation of why the query is still running.

This compounds the finding above: the one message that most needs to be read (a write-gate rejection) is also the one with the shortest life. Note the round-2 fix that introduced this clearing was correct in intent — a stale error must not outlive the condition — but tying it to the poll rather than to the next kill attempt overshoots.
issues.fix_hint: Clear killError at the start of the next kill (already done) and on a successful kill, rather than on any successful poll. If a poll-driven clear is still wanted for the case where the row disappeared on its own, scope it to when the errored id is no longer present in the fresh list.
issues.title: killError is cleared by the very next successful poll, so a kill failure is visible for under 2 seconds

issues.body:
`registryHeaders` sends `token?.trim()` and both callers pass `endpointToken.trim() || undefined`, so "secret" and "secret " produce an identical request. But the reset effect compares `current.token !== endpointToken` on the raw value, so appending a trailing space to the token field unmounts EndpointQueryMonitor and the user has to click "Monitor endpoint" again for a request that would have been byte-identical. The url side is already normalized (the parent passes `endpointUrl.trim()`); the token side is not.

Related and equally small: the teardown is silent. The panel reverts to "Server-side monitoring is opt-in and starts only when requested", which reads as if it was never started.
issues.fix_hint: Normalize both sides once — pass `endpointToken.trim()` down from PlanExplorer, or compare `current.token.trim() !== endpointToken.trim()`. Optionally render a one-line muted note when a running monitor is auto-stopped by an endpoint edit, so the disappearance is explained rather than inferred.
issues.title: The auto-stop effect compares the token untrimmed while the fetch helpers trim it, so a whitespace-only edit silently tears down monitoring

issues.body:
`endpointRegistryMessage` returns `retry: true` for anything that is not a recognized QueryRegistryHttpError status. A server that goes away, a DNS failure, or a CORS rejection therefore leaves a red `[data-plan-endpoint-monitor-error]` line while the component re-fetches on a fixed 2s cadence for as long as the tab stays open. The 404/405 and 401/403 cases are correctly terminal; only the open-ended one is unbounded.

Low impact — it is opt-in, points only at the configured endpoint, and stops on unmount — but it is a quiet background loop with no ceiling. It also interacts with the row-parse issue below: one unparseable row makes every subsequent poll fail the same way, so the loop never converges.
issues.fix_hint: Add a modest backoff (2s doubling to ~30s) or a consecutive-failure cap after which the chain stops and the message offers a re-arm, resetting the counter on the next success alongside the existing setKillError(null).
issues.title: A generic (non-HTTP) poll failure retries every 2s indefinitely with no backoff or attempt cap

issues.body:
`parseRegistryRow` returns null for any row it does not fully recognize, and `fetchEndpointRunningQueries` then throws "invalid row" for the whole response. Today that is exactly right — the server emits only kind "query" and "update" (RegistryEntry::kind in crates/sparq-server/src/http.rs) and the field set matches QueryRegistry::list exactly. But it means a future server that adds a third kind, or a single odd row, blanks the entire monitor into a red error that (per the previous item) then retries forever, instead of showing the rows it could parse.

This is a deliberate strictness choice and defensible; flagging it as forward-compat brittleness rather than a defect.
issues.fix_hint: Drop unparseable rows and render the ones that parsed (optionally with a muted "n rows not understood" note), reserving the hard throw for a malformed envelope. If the closed `kind` set is meant to be strict, a comment saying so — and that widening it is a server-coordinated change — would make the intent explicit.
issues.title: One unrecognized row fails the entire list rather than degrading, and `kind` is validated as a closed set

issues.body:
Two small things in the same helper.

(1) `parseRegistryRow` requires `start` to be a finite number and the interface documents it as Unix epoch ms, but no consumer uses it — EndpointMonitorRow renders only kind, fingerprint and elapsed_ms. The validation is harmless and correctly matches the server's `started_at_unix_ms`, but a stricter check on an unused field will reject a future server that legitimately omits it.

(2) `registryUrl` pops the last path segment and appends `queries`, documented as "assume the registry is a sibling of the SPARQL endpoint". The server mounts `/queries` at the ROOT, so any deployment where the SPARQL route is nested more than one level (e.g. `/api/v1/sparql`) derives `/api/v1/queries` and gets a 404 — which the UI then reports as "Server-side registry not enabled (start sparq-server with --features query-registry)", sending the operator after the wrong problem.
issues.fix_hint: For (1): either use it (an absolute start time in the row's `title` complements the relative elapsed readout) or drop it from the interface and the required-field check, leaving elapsed_ms as the single time source. For (2): widen the 404 copy to name both causes ("registry not enabled, or /queries is not reachable at <derived url>") and include the derived URL, so a path-prefix mismatch is self-diagnosing.
issues.title: EndpointRunningQuery.start is validated but never read, and the sibling-path heuristic can misdiagnose a 404 as "feature not enabled"

verdict.summary:
No blocker or major. I verified the server contract rather than assuming it: crates/sparq-server/src/http.rs mounts GET /queries (list_queries_handler, READ-gated) and DELETE /queries/{id} (cancel_query_handler, WRITE-gated) behind the non-default `query-registry` feature, and QueryRegistry::list emits exactly {id, kind, start, fingerprint, elapsed_ms} with kind in {"query","update"} — parseRegistryRow matches field-for-field. The meta.ts / header rewrite from "needs net-new machinery" to "opt-in /queries registry" is therefore honest, and the 404 copy names the exact flag.

Security edges hold. killEndpointRunningQuery encodes the id (a test pins queries/query%2Fid, so a slash cannot traverse the path), registryUrl rejects non-http(s) schemes, and the token gate uses the right discriminator (code === "token-over-plaintext" && level === "warning"), so the benign loopback-http info note does not disable monitoring while a real non-loopback plaintext token does — both directions have an e2e. Opt-in is pinned by request ABSENCE (expect(listCalls).toBe(0)), not UI absence. Unit tests are non-vacuous: URL derivation, prefix preservation, header/method, signal identity, status exposure, both malformed shapes.

I re-walked the async paths and found nothing material: the poll chain keeps one timeout slot, requestSequence drops stale kill/poll setState without stalling the chain, abort short-circuits every setState, and the effect deps are immutable snapshot fields.

Progress is stagnant, not improving: HEAD is still 414cb811 ("address review round 2") and the diff is byte-identical to what round 3 reviewed, so all five round-3 items remain. My list is the same class — test-strength and message polish — plus one killError lifetime issue compounding round 3's kill-message finding.

Tests were assessed by reading only; gui/app/node_modules is absent here, so `node --test` and the Playwright lane could not be run.
